This program is accepted industry-wide for dynamic stability analysis. 2.3 Base Cases 2.3.1 Power Flow Analysis (Steady State) Base cases used in the thermal and voltage analysis for this study were developed based upon the expected topology for the local area in the summer of 2018 (near term model chosen by MISO) and for the summer of 2025 (out-year model chosen by MISO).

It should be noted that the 2018 model contained the Badger Coulee 345-kV line which is not expected to be entirely in-service by June 2018, but is a required contingent project for other MISO Generator Interconnection Requests west of the DPP-Wisconsin study area and is therefore required to be modeled in the near term case per MISO procedures.
The ATC footprint in these cases was updated with the most recent data available at the time of model construction.
megawatts: Dane County, WI J390 – 702 MW Combined Cycle Natural Gas Generation;
Rock County, WI J395 – 98 MW Wind Generation;
The queued request is to increase the Energy Resource Interconnection Service (ERIS) and Network Resource Interconnection Service (NRIS) of the plant by 21 MW to a new summer capability of 489 MW.
The queued request is for 702 MW of new ERIS and NRIS summer capability.
The queued request is for 98 MW of new ERIS summer capability.

As shown in Table B.1 in Appendix B, J395 will be restricted to a maximum of: 1. 75 MW at the machine terminals 2. 75 MW at the machine terminals This issue will be investigated in further detail prior to J395’s plans for initial synchronization;

The only prior queued requests in the ATC footprint are J061, J241, and J382, a 70 MW wind farm in Delta County, Michigan, a 3.7 MW hydro generation increase in Dickinson County, Michigan, and a 48.3 MW natural gas simple cycle NRIS only request in Dane County, Wisconsin, respectively.
Also of note is J293, a 475 MW natural gas combined cycle request in Outagamie County, Wisconsin which terminated its GIA during the analysis of the February 2015 DPP study cycle.
J394 is a 280/327 MW (summer/winter) natural gas combined cycle plant located in Marquette County, Michigan.
This 489 MW amount reflects a 21 MW increase at the POI from the existing Interconnection Service of J384.
in_service: The 2018 Shoulder load case will not solve without the Badger Coulee project in-service, however, the 2025 model with the Cardinal Hickory Creek in-service indicates an increase in flow of approximately 15 MVA on X-49 without Badger Coulee.

The 2018 Shoulder load case will not solve without the Badger Coulee project in-service, however, the 2025 model with the Cardinal Hickory Creek in-service indicates an increase in flow of 3-4 MVA on Y-155 without Badger Coulee.
location: J384 is an existing three-unit simple cycle natural gas fired power plant in Dane County, Wisconsin known as RockGen Energy Center connected to the Christiana 138-kV Substation (see Figure 1).

J390 is a proposed three-unit (two combustion turbines and a heat recovery steam generating unit) combined cycle, natural gas fired generation plant requesting to site in Rock County, Wisconsin at the existing Townline Road 138-kV Substation (see Figure 1).
J395 is a proposed wind farm requesting to site in Lafayette County, Wisconsin at a new 138-kV substation connected to the Hillman-Darlington 138-kV Line X-14.

Based on the power factor requirement analysis in Section 3.8, J395 is required to install additional reactive compensation beyond the inherent power factor capability of the Generating Facility such that the wind farm is capable of meeting ATC’s standard power factor range of 0.90 lagging (providing VArs) to 0.95 leading (absorbing VArs) at the POI.
Section 1.4.1 describes the Network Upgrades necessary for the study group with J390 at its requested, 138-kV POI.
Section 1.4.2 describes the Network Upgrades necessary for the study group with J390 at the alternate 345-kV POI. 1.4.1 Network Upgrades:
cost: Analysis of J390 at the 138-kV POI led to an overall cost to interconnect the February 2015 DPP-Wisconsin group of approximately $143.7 million.

Analysis of J390 at the 345-kV POI led to an overall cost to interconnect the February 2015 DPP-Wisconsin group of $82 million; a $61.7 million reduction with equal or greater transmission system reliability.
One is estimated to cost $7.0 million with an 18-24 month construction period, the other is an existing ComEd baseline project expected to be in-service by the summer of 2019.

The Townline Road Substation expansion costs include $204,329.34 (the Phase I Facility Study indicated a cost of $180,000 for this work which was then escalated to 2020 dollars in this report) for this analysis and equipment.
This work is estimated to cost $5.8 million.
This work is estimated to cost $159,135.
owner: Power Factor Requirement, Synchronous Generators FERC Order ER05-1475 requires all synchronous generators interconnecting to ATC-owned Facilities to provide a power factor capability of 0.90 lagging (providing VArs) to 0.95 leading (absorbing VArs) at the POI.

This program is accepted industry-wide for dynamic stability analysis. 2.3 Base Cases 2.3.1 Power Flow Analysis (Steady State) Base cases used in the thermal and voltage analysis for this study were developed based upon the expected topology for the local area in the summer of 2018 (near term model chosen by MISO) and for the summer of 2025 (out-year model chosen by MISO).

American Transmission Company 74 6/8/2016 February 2015 DPPAppendix D Exhibit System Wisconsin Interconnection 1 Impact Study These events were tested again with independent pole operated (IPO) breakers modeled at the Townline Road 345kV substation and the instability is resolved.

MODELS AND ASSUMPTIONS Power flow models representing the near-term (2018) and out-year (2025) system topology with summer peak load forecasts were developed from the ERIS study models for this group.

Thus, adding this amount of RER capacity to the three previously approved RER contracts would exceed the 25 MW program cap established by the Commission in 2017.

It thus set a cap of 25 MW, which was equivalent to 5.0 percent of total system coincident peak demand, stating “[i]t is easier to set an initial cap, and increase the cap when necessary, th[a]n it is to forgo setting a cap and imposing one at a later date.” Id. at 10-11.
MGE will have reached the 25 MW participation limit in fewer than three years with the approval of this project, and, as anticipated by the Commission, an increase to the RER program cap is required.

megawatts: Throughout this Application new large loads refer to customers that exceed 100 MW in size, a definition consistent with recent Commission decisions. 1 Such customers could bring substantial property taxes, workforce opportunities, and regional economic benefits.
In addition, the Company estimates in this Application that the addition of 500 MW of customer load can reduce existing customer rates by up to 2 percent.

The Company also estimates that 500 MW of additional load through the new tariff could bring $490 to $630 million in benefits to communities in the form of taxes and existing customer rate relief over the life of the proposed 15-year initial term of service.
In other Xcel Energy jurisdictions, though, the Company has material requests from non-data center large customers with loads exceeding 100 MW.

Large General Service Time-of-Day Service (Cg-9) 3 Cg-9 is mandatory for customers with demand equal to or greater than 200 kW for 4 of 12 months at any voltage of service and constitutes the Company’s largest standard tariff for large customers. 2.
Real Time Pricing Service (RTP-1) RTP-1 is optional for customers with demand equal to or greater than 1,000 kW at any voltage of service.
The tariff has a limit of 140,000 kW of enrolled customer load. 3.

The Company is not currently considering raising the cap on RTP-1 and, as such, does not believe RTP-1 is a feasible tariff for new large customers given the current cap effectively limits enrollment of a new 100 MW customer.
As discussed later in this Application, the Company is proposing to prohibit participation in the CMP-1 tariff by new large customers exceeding 100 MW eligible for the Large Load Tariff.
The Company’s analysis considers adding a hypothetical 500 MW new large customer enrolled in the Cg-9 tariff to the Company’s as-filed 2027 test year rate case.

documents.title: 05-AE-243 Application to Sell 100 MW of Riverside to WEPCO

megawatts: Stat. § 196.80 for WPSC to sell its 100 MW interest in West Riverside to Wisconsin Electric, and to assign to Wisconsin Electric all WPSC’s contractual rights and obligations in West Riverside.

The Applicants have determined that including 100 MW of West Riverside’s capacity in Wisconsin Electric’s generating portfolio will assist Wisconsin Electric in meeting its obligations, and will provide net economic benefits to customers.

West Riverside is a highly efficient natural gas combined cycle electric generating facility, which consists of:  Two advanced technology combustion turbines, designated as Unit 1 and Unit 2 (232.9 MW per unit);  Two heat recovery, steam generators;  One steam turbine (257.4 MW); and  One solar facility (4 MW).
Together, the units have a nameplate capacity of 727.2 MW.

In addition, without transferring 100 MW of capacity from WPSC to Wisconsin Electric, and assuming all else remains equal with respect to the GRP, Wisconsin Electric would be short of capacity, and WPSC would be long.
Thus, allowing Wisconsin Electric to acquire the 100 MW share of West Riverside from WPSC is consistent with the public interest, as required by Wis.
The proposed transaction will transfer ownership from WPSC of approximately 100 MW of nameplate capacity to Wisconsin Electric.
WPSC owns or has under contract 2,482 MW of -7- capacity and Wisconsin Electric owns or has under contract 5,693 MW of capacity.
This change in ownership will have a de minimis effect on competition considering the approximately 134,000 MW of capacity available in the MISO market.
Adding 100 MW of nameplate generating capacity to Wisconsin Electric’s portfolio will give the company approximately 4.32% of the region’s total generating capacity, an increase of 0.07%.
in_service: Located near Beloit, Wisconsin, West Riverside achieved commercial operation on May 14, 2020.

equipment_maker_model: The EGEAS model and key modeling parameters and assumptions used in the EGEAS model are described below. 4.1 EGEAS Utility Planning Model MGE used the EGEAS utility planning model to evaluate the relative cost-effectiveness and performance of alternative plans for meeting MGE’s customers’ future electric supply needs under various potential futures.
MGE has used the EGEAS utility planning model since the early 1990’s.
EGEAS is a computer software model developed by the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI).

Inputs to the EGEAS model related to new and existing generating units include for example, but are not limited to, generating unit size, heat rate, operating costs, capital costs, maintenance requirements, construction schedules, unit retirement schedules, emission rates, emission allowance pricing, and hourly generation profiles for non-dispatchable renewable technologies.
location: Section 3.2 of this report describes the different alterative plans that MGE evaluated as part of its analysis of MGE’s future electric supply needs. 3.1.2 Future A “future” is defined as a complete set of specified “uncertainties” that may play out or unfold over time.

Section 3.3 of this report describes the various futures that MGE evaluated as part of its analysis of MGE’s future electric supply needs. 3.1.3 Scenario A “scenario” is defined as a complete set of specified variables (both “options” and “uncertainties”).

Section 3.4 of this report describes the various scenarios that MGE evaluated as part of its analysis of MGE’s future electric supply needs. 3.1.4 Sensitivity Sensitivity analysis is a means of testing the extent to which the results of an analysis may change if one or more of the assumptions used in the analysis were to change.

Section 6 of this report describes the various sensitivity runs that MGE performed to test the robustness of the analysis results. 3.2 Development of Alternative Plans The following unique alternative plans were identified for the current round of EGEAS analyses.

MGE’s base set of files have been designated as its “a” series of files (see section 4.25 for more information on the EGEAS filing naming convention used by MGE to keep track of the different series of EGEAS files used to complete each scenario and sensitivity run).
owner: Other scenarios and sensitivities that MGE examined included, for example, the exercise of MGE’s option to participate in ownership in the Riverside Energy Center Expansion (RECE) project; the possibility of carbon constraints; and a possible future with carbon constraints, higher natural gas prices, and higher energy market prices.
EGEAS is a computer software model developed by the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI).

equipment_maker_model: By analyzing these two unique plans, the EGEAS model can be used to estimate the incremental costs of installing a particular planning alternative across a variety of futures.

The EGEAS model and key modeling parameters and assumptions used in the EGEAS model are described below. 4.1 EGEAS Utility Planning Model MGE used the EGEAS utility planning model to evaluate the relative cost-effectiveness and performance of alternative plans for meeting MGE’s customers’ future electric supply needs under various potential futures.
MGE has used the EGEAS utility planning model since the early 1990’s.
EGEAS is a computer software model developed by the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI).

Inputs to the EGEAS model related to new and existing generating units include for example, but are not limited to, generating unit size, heat rate (efficiency), operating costs, capital costs, maintenance requirements, construction schedules, unit retirement schedules, emission rates, emission allowance pricing, and hourly generation profiles for non-dispatchable renewable technologies.
This new model allows MGE to partner with business customers – including those looking to relocate or expand in the MGE service territory.

(a) during the facility’s first two years of operation, MGE has the option to purchase up to 25 MW of West Riverside nameplate capacity; and (b) during the third, fourth, and fifth years of operation, MGE has the option to purchase up to a cumulative 50 MW of West Riverside nameplate capacity.

equipment_maker_model: The PLEXOS model provides the most robust model functionality and is a proven power market simulation tool that is a leader in modeling flexibility, efficiency, simulation alternatives and advanced analysis.

equipment_maker_model: The PLEXOS model provides the most robust model functionality and is a proven power market simulation tool that is a leader in modeling flexibility, efficiency, simulation alternatives and advanced analysis.

In addition, the support, continuous improvements, and its capability to perform both fuel budget runs and capacity expansion simulations made this model the obvious choice for WEC when it came time to replace the long-term capacity expansion modeling.

The Rock River flows into the Town of Beloit in the Town’s northeast corner (Section 1) near Riverside Drive (USH 51) and the Alliant Energy Facility, and flows north-south through the Town, into the City of Beloit and on to Rockford, IL. before continuing southwest to meet the Mississippi River near the Quad Cities.

Elevations range from as little as 740 feet above sea level along the Rock River and in the extreme southwest corner of the Town (Section 31) to as high as 945 feet above sea level near Creedy Rd (SW Section 8).
Located in Rock County at the intersection of Interstates 39/90 and 43, Beloit has large areas of newer commercial and industrial activities as well as an historic downtown along the Rock River.
Centered at the junction of Interstates 39/90 and 43, the City of Beloit is located on a direct route to many of the Midwest’s major population, economic, and innovation centers.
cost: The cost of vacant residential lots in the City varies widely, from approximately $10,000 in the central City to as high as $50,000 in neighborhoods with larger, executive-style homes along Turtle Creek.
At the City-sponsored Housing Conference in August 2017, one of the presenters estimated the cost of developing a typical single-family lot (including water, sewer, gas, etc.) to be $20K to $25K.

equipment_maker_model: The Facility is an existing generation facility consisting of two General Electric (“GE”) model 7FA.03 combustion turbines (“CTs”), two heat recovery steam generators (“HRSGs”) and a single steam turbine generator (“STG”) in combined cycle configuration.

Each CT generator set consists of a hydrogen-cooled generator supplied by GE, an inlet air system, a starting system, a natural gas fuel supply system, a cooling water system, a fire protection system, an exhaust system with PUBLIC VERSION silencing, and other subsystems as required for safe and reliable operations.
The Project involves replacing the existing CTs (GE 7FA.03), including the rotors, and upgrading them to the current model (GE 7FA.05).

This replacement involves removal of the existing 7FA.03 combustion turbine, excluding the generator and various BOP systems, installation of a complete 7FA.05 CT, which will have the effect of increasing accredited capacity and improving efficiency of the facility for WPL’s customers.
The GE 7FA.05 CTs described in Section 1.1.4 are natural gas-fired CTs.
Long-lead, and therefore critical path, major equipment items are expected to include the latest GE model 7FA.05.

WPL is negotiating an amendment to its existing contractual service agreement with GE which contains provisions for the purchase of the 7FA.05 package with equipment delivery dates aligned with the proposed Project timeline. 2.4.6.

case_pages.title: Application of the Village of French Island for Authority to be a Public Water Utility, Construct and Acquire Facilities from the Campbell Water Utility, and Provide Water Service to Customers in the Former Town of Campbell, in the Village of French Island, La Crosse County, Wisconsin.
case_pages.summary: The Village of French Island is seeking approval for the construction of a new water system including: a new well, a distribution system, elevated storage tank, pumphouse/water treatment facilities, and well site sewer upgrades for the French Island Water System. Properties with private wells would be required to abandon the existing private wells when service becomes available to avoid system contamination. The Village of French Island is also seeking approval to acquire the facilities from the Campbell Water Utility and to provide service to customers in the former Town of Campbell, now residents of the Village of French Island, due to the incorporation of the town to the now Village of French Island. This incorporation has resulted in the proposed project, previously proposed in docket 935-CW-102, to be transferred to the current docket 6812-CW-100. The project design has not changed and is functionally identical to the project previously referred to as the Campbell Water System project. Applicant Stated Need The project is needed to provide safe drinking water for village residents. The majority of village residents currently source drinking water from private wells. Wisconsin DNR issued a water advisory advising residents that the groundwater is not fit for human consumption due to potential human health risks. This project would provide a safer alternative water supply. Estimated Cost The applicant states that the estimated project cost is $55,815,895. The Village proposes requiring residents to abandon private wells and connect to the new distribution system when service becomes available to them. The applicant proposes requiring residents to pay the associated costs, but is also seeking funding programs available for these costs. Project Location The project would be located in the Village of French Island in La Crosse County, Wisconsin. Proposed Schedule The Town of Campbell submitted the original application to the Commission in October 2025. The town has since incorporated as the Village of French Island. The previous docket 935-CW-102 has been closed to allow for the Village of French Island (applicant) to create the current docket. The Village of French Island submitted the updated application for the proposed project to the Commission in July 2026. If approved and all necessary permits are acquired, the applicant anticipates construction for this project to begin December 1, 2026 with an estimated completion date of May 15, 2029. Statutory Re

case_pages.title: Application of Columbia Project, LLC for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity to Construct, Install, and Operate a Wind Electric Generating Facility Capable of Generating Up to 277 MW, Known as the Columbia Wind Project in the Towns of Columbus, Hampden, Leeds, Fountain Prairie, Lowville, Otsego, Courtland, Springvale and the Village of Doylestown, Columbia County, Wisconsin
case_pages.summary: Columbia Project LLC, an indirect subsidiary of Alliant Energy Finance LLC, is seeking approval to construct a wind energy generating facility with a generating capacity of 277.3 MWac (megawatt alternating current) in the Towns of Columbus, Hampden, Leeds, Fountain Prairie, Lowville, Ostego, Courtland, Springvale, and the Village of Doylestown in Columbia County, Wisconsin. The project area consists of 48,377 acres of mostly agricultural land. Of these 48,377 acres, approximately 779 acres of temporary ground disturbance impacts are expected during construction of the project, and approximately 100 acres will host the long-term operational facilities of the project. The major components of the proposed project include up to 47 wind turbines, approximately 88 miles of underground 34.5 kilovolt (kV) collector circuits, a 345 kV collector substation, up to three meteorological towers, an aircraft detection lighting system tower, access roads, and an operation and maintenance building. The project proposal includes a total of 59 turbine locations, with 47 proposed wind turbine locations and 12 alternative wind turbine locations. Individual wind turbines can be identified by their identification number. View the Interactive Project Map or download the Project Map . Applicant Stated Need This project is proposed by an affiliate of a public utility. The Commission must grant approval for the affiliate to own and operate the proposed facility, however, if granted the need for the project is not reviewed by the Commission. This type of work is referred to as an “uprate” and can include modifications such as: Structure replacement. Modification of structures to increase attachment/structure height. Modification to location of clamp along conductors (“Slip and Clip"). Areas of transmission line where modifications would be performed to achieve the uprate are referred to within the application’s tables and maps as “S-Mod” or “N-Mod.” Uprate work would include replacement of approximately 65 structures in the north scope, and replacement of 21 to 31 structures in the south scope. case_pages.summary: American Transmission Company (ATC or applicant) is seeking approval to construct a second 345 kilovolt (kV) transmission line between the existing Elm Road Substation in Milwaukee County and the existing Racine Substation in Racine County. The south portion of ATC’s existing 138 kV Oak Creek to Racine transmission line (Line 812) would be converted to 345 kV and re-terminated into the Racine Substation 345 kV bus. The remaining portion of the line would be retired. Approximately 3.7 miles of new 345 kV line would be built on new right-of-way (ROW) to connect the converted portion of Line 812 to the Elm Road Substation. The Proposed Route would be 2.2 miles in length including a total of 39.1 acres of ROW, of which 14.2 acres would be new ROW. The Alternate Route would be 2.4 miles in length including a total of 43.1 acres of ROW, of which 23.4 acres would be new ROW. The Common Route (not including Segment R) would be 2.4 miles in length including a total of 44.5 acres of ROW, of which 26.4 acres would be new ROW. Common Route Segment R is an existing corridor that is approximately 8.2 miles in length and no physical work would be performed; therefore, it would not involve acquiring any new ROW. The project would include modifications to the Elm Road Substation and the Racine Substation, however neither would be expanded and all substation work would occur within the existing substation footprints. A new 345 kV breaker would be installed at the Elm Road Substation, and new 345 kV breakers and buses would be installed at the Racine Substation. The proposed project would also acquire easements over the narrow strips of land between ATC’s existing 230 kV and 345 kV transmission corridors and the proposed transmission corridor for the project. The applicant states this is to ensure a safe topple distance between existing transmission structures and the new proposed structures, to improve construction and maintenance access, and to avoid the creation of uneconomic remnants for landowners. These easement acquisitions are Segment U (Proposed Route) containing approximately 4.5 acres, Segment V (Alternate Route) containing approximately 2.9 acres, and Segment T (Common Route) containing approximately 4.9 acres. Applicant Stated Need The project is needed for additional capacity in the Elm Road to Racine corridor to allow new loads and generators to reliably interconnect to the system. case_pages.title: Application of American Transmission Company LLC, as an Electric Public Utility, for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity to Construct and Operate the Western Feed Transmission Line Project, Consisting of Two Sets of Double-Circuit 345 kV Transmission Lines, One Set of Double-Circuit 138/345 kV, and One Single-Circuit 345 kV to Interconnect the New Jupiter and Cosmos Distribution Substations Located Primarily in the Villages of Yorkville and Mount Pleasant, Racine County.
case_pages.summary: American Transmission Company (ATC or applicant) is seeking approval to construct two new substations, named the Jupiter and Cosmos substations, and multiple new transmission lines to interconnect the new substations to existing facilities. Each substation would have a 33.5-acre site. Two new double-circuit 345 kilovolt (kV) transmission lines would connect ATC’s existing Paris-Arcadian 345 kV line (W-30) and Pleasant Prairie-Arcadian 345 kV line (PLPL81) to the new Jupiter and Cosmos substations. New 138/345 kV double-circuit transmission lines would interconnect the new Cosmos substation to ATC’s existing Mount Pleasant substation. The project would also require a new 345 kV single-circuit transmission line, which would be designed for an ultimate double-circuit configuration, to interconnect the new Jupiter substation to ATC’s existing Mount Pleasant substation. The Proposed Route would be 3.6 miles in length including a total Right-of-Way (ROW) of approximately 152 acres. The Alternative Route would be 3.7 miles in length including a total of 159 acres of ROW. The Common Route would be 6.0 miles in length including a total of 171 acres of ROW. The routes are occurring almost entirely within new ROW, ranging between 0 percent shared and 3 percent shared with existing ROW depending on the route. Applicant stated need The project is needed to support multiple large new load additions within the Electronics and Information Technology Manufacturing Zone (EITMZ) requested by We Energies in southeastern Wisconsin. Estimated cost The applicant stated that the estimated project cost would be approximately $593.8 million if the proposed route is selected and approximately $621.9 million if the alternative route is selected. Project location The project would be located in the Villages of Yorkville, Mount Pleasant, and Sturtevant in Racine County, Wisconsin. Proposed schedule The applicant submitted the application to the Commission in July 2024. If approved, the applicant anticipates construction for this project to begin in November of 2025 and be completed by December of 2026 for the transmission lines, and by June of 2028 for the new substations. Statutory Review The proposed project is categorized as a Type II action under Wis. Admin. Code § PSC 4.10(2) . The Commission prepared an Environmental Assessment (EA) for this project that evaluated the location of the project and its potential environmental, community, and private property impacts. case_pages.summary: Wisconsin Electric Gas Operations (WE-GO), doing business as We Energies, is seeking approval to construct a new 33-mile natural gas transmission pipeline in southeast Wisconsin. The project is new construction that consists of a 24-inch and 30-inch steel 650 pounds per square inch gauge (psig) maximum allowable operating pressure (MAOP) transmission main to tie supply and load together from the existing WE-GO Bluff Creek Liquified Natural Gas Facility to the combined Oak Creek and Elm Road Generating Station (ERGS) campus. The proposed project is described as having two potential routes, “Route A" and “Route B". Approximately 7 percent of the gas pipeline on Route A would be located within public road right-of-way (ROW), and approximately 5 percent for Route B. Some private land would be utilized for the gas pipeline ROW. The typical proposed permanent easement width is 50 feet; however, the final proposed easement widths along the proposed routes will be finalized during the easement negotiation process. Estimated cost The applicant has stated that the estimated project cost is $210,942,310 for Route A and $217,093,529 for Route B. case_pages.summary: Madison Gas and Electric (MGE or the applicant) is seeking approval to construct a solar energy generating facility with a generating capacity of 20 megawatts (MW) alternating current (AC) plus a 40 MW battery energy storage system (BESS) in the City of Fitchburg in Dane County. case_pages.title: Joint Application of Northern States Power Company-Wisconsin and American Transmission Company LLC, as Electric Public Utilities, for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity to Rebuild Existing Transmission Infrastructure and Construct and Operate LRTP Tranche 1 Project 5, which consists of Expanding the Tremval and Eau Claire Substations, a New Jump River Substation, and a New 345 kV Transmission Line connecting the Tremval-Eau Claire-Jump River Substations, in the Counties of Chippewa, Clark, Eau Claire, and Trempealeau, Wisconsin, to be known as the Western Wisconsin Transmission Connection Project.
case_pages.summary: Northern States Power Company – Wisconsin (Xcel Energy) and American Transmission Company (ATC), together as the applicants, are seeking a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) approval to construct a new 345 kV (kilovolt) high voltage transmission line (HVTL) in the counties of Chippewa, Clark, Eau Claire, and Trempealeau, Wisconsin. The project would also rebuild existing lines, construct new 345 kV substations depending on the chosen transmission route, and expand or upgrade multiple existing substations. The project proposes two potential routes, Route 1 and Route 2, that share a common segment at the southern portion of the project. The project would start at an expansion of the existing Tremval Substation near the Town of Blair in Trempealeau County and run north to the east of Eau Claire where the two proposed routes diverge. Route 1 would proceed west into Eau Claire, then northeast to end at the proposed Jump River Substation North near Sheldon in Chippewa County. Route 2 would interconnect with the proposed Elk Farm Substation and proceed east, turn north, then east until ending at the proposed Jump River South Substation in Clark County. The Proposed Route 1 would be approximately 94 miles in length including a total of 1,678 acres of Right-of-Way (ROW). The Proposed Route 2 would be approximately 80 miles in length including a total of 1,450 acres of ROW. The Common Segment between both routes would be approximately 40 miles in length including a total of 708 to 712 acres of ROW, depending on the chosen route. Route 1 would share 64 percent of its total ROW with existing ROW, and Route 2 would share 38 percent with existing ROW. Applicant stated need The project is one part of the MISO Long-Range Transmission Planning (LRTP) Tranche 1 Portfolio of projects (this project is specifically LRTP Project 5) recommended to meet transmission system reliability, economic, and public policy needs. The applicants state the project would fill a need for a reliable transmission grid to support future generation resources and future load. The project would allow for the interconnection of new renewable energy sources as fossil-fuel generation sources are retired. Additionally, the project would reduce load on multiple facilities in northern and northwestern Wisconsin. case_pages.summary: Northern States Power Company-Wisconsin (NSPW) is proposing construction of a new electric generation facility with a total nameplate capacity of 255 MW. Major components of the project include one F-class Combustion Turbine (CT) generator (210 MW) and five Reciprocating Internal Combustion Engine (RICE) units (9 MW each), which would all be capable of operating with natural gas or No. 2 fuel oil. The facilities would also include accessory structures for water preparation and storage, fuel storage and handling, electrical interconnection, and other support functions. The CT and RICE units would be interconnected to the existing onsite interconnection point currently utilized by Wheaton Units 1-4 and 6, which would be retired in conjunction with the proposed project.
